record.paper_title: Reusing Space: Techniques and Open Problems
record.original_question: Can one devise a circuit that uses techniques from space reuse or catalytic computing to solve some problem efficiently in a way that is not currently known directly in the circuit model?

evidence.quote: Problem 27. Devise a circuit that uses techniques from space reuse and catalytic computing to solve some problem in low size or depth in a way that we do not know how to do directly.

artifact.self_contained_problem:
Background. In catalytic computation one considers a Turing machine equipped with two work tapes: a small "clean" work tape of size s(n), initially blank, and an additional "auxiliary" (catalytic) tape of size c(n), initialized with an arbitrary (worst-case) string τ. The machine may freely read and write the catalytic tape during its computation, but at the end of the computation the catalytic tape must again contain exactly the initial string τ, for every choice of τ. The class CSPACE(s(n), c(n)) consists of languages decided by such machines, and CL = CSPACE(O(log n), 2^{O(log n)}). It is known that uniform TC^1 ⊆ CL, even though no direct simulation of CL by small uniform circuits is known.

Problem. Exhibit an explicit family of Boolean circuits C = {C_n} computing some specific function f : {0,1}^* → {0,1} such that:
(a) the construction of C_n is obtained by translating a catalytic-computation or space-reuse algorithm (i.e., one that crucially exploits being able to reuse cells that hold arbitrary "junk" data and to restore them) into the circuit model; and
(b) the resulting circuit family achieves a size bound s(n) or depth bound d(n) for f that is strictly better than any known bound for f obtained by direct circuit-model techniques (without going through space reuse or catalytic computing).

In other words, produce a concrete example where catalytic / space-reuse ideas yield a new upper bound on circuit size or depth that is not currently achievable by purely circuit-based methods.
artifact.status_search_result: Recent surveys and papers on catalytic computing (2024–2025), including work on lossy catalytic computation, the structure of catalytic space, and quantum catalytic space, continue to list the interaction between catalytic-space techniques and circuit upper bounds as an active and unresolved direction. Known containments such as TC^1 ⊆ CL and SAC^2 inside near-polynomial catalytic space go from circuits into catalytic space, but no example is reported of a new circuit upper bound obtained via catalytic / space-reuse techniques beyond what is known directly. The problem appears to remain open.

status_evidence.title: Catalytic computing - Wikipedia
status_evidence.snippet: Uniform TC^1 circuits are computable in catalytic logspace; understanding CL remains a major open problem.
status_evidence.claim: Catalytic-space techniques have yielded simulations of circuit classes by catalytic machines, but the converse direction (new circuit bounds from catalytic ideas) is not established.

status_evidence.title: Quantum Catalytic Space (arXiv:2506.16324)
status_evidence.snippet: Recent (2025) work extends catalytic computation; classical analogues of efficient simulations remain the largest open questions.
status_evidence.claim: Active recent research indicates the area's central questions, including circuit-model payoffs of catalytic techniques, remain open.

status_evidence.title: Fully Characterizing Lossy Catalytic Computation (ECCC TR24-138)
status_evidence.snippet: Continued investigation of the power of catalytic space and its relation to standard complexity classes.
status_evidence.claim: Recent results refine the understanding of catalytic space but do not exhibit a circuit family beating direct circuit constructions via space-reuse techniques.
